children.text: Our focus: large, high-quality gemstones

Our gemstone buying is limited to large, high-quality stones. Green Colombian emeralds, Burmese rubies from Myanmar and Ceylon blue sapphires from Sri Lanka are examples of our focus. Certificates are welcome but not required. Describe what you have so we can discuss an appropriate evaluation.
This is separate from our diamond buying: we buy natural, cut and polished diamonds of any size or shape. We do not buy laboratory-grown, uncut or rough diamonds.
Start with what you know about the ring

Write down the name used on the original receipt, any markings inside the band, and repairs you know about. Describe an unknown stone as unknown. A blue stone is not enough evidence to call a ring a sapphire, and a family description does not establish a geographic origin.

Bring the ring intact. The setting may limit what can be measured or examined, but removing the stone at home can damage both parts. Ask what can be assessed while it is mounted and whether further examination would meaningfully change the purchase decision.
Discuss the gemstone and the setting separately
Stone size alone does not explain quality. For example,
GIA's sapphire guide
discusses color, clarity, cut and carat weight. Different gemstone varieties need their own assessment; a diamond grading scale cannot simply be applied to every colored stone.

children.text: Ask which identification or treatment information is known, which comes from a report, and which remains uncertain. Then ask how the metal, accent diamonds, maker's marks and condition of the ring affect the total offer. Our
sapphire and diamond jewelry guide
covers pieces with more than one type of stone.
Organize the paperwork without buying unnecessary reports

Keep the laboratory report with the matching ring. A purchase receipt, insurance schedule and repair invoice can each add context, but they serve different purposes. If you cannot match a document confidently, bring it and explain the uncertainty.
Bring existing reports and the original sales description, if available.
Note a chipped stone, loose setting, resizing or replacement stone.
Keep any original box and detached parts with the ring.
Photograph the item for your own inventory before the visit.
Ask whether an additional laboratory report is useful before paying for one. Its cost and turnaround should make sense for the actual piece and your reason for selling.
A purchase offer answers a different question from an appraisal
A purchase offer states what a buyer is prepared to pay under the stated terms. A formal appraisal identifies its purpose and valuation basis.
GIA's appraisal guidance
explains that GIA grades and identifies gems but does not assign their monetary value.

For an insurance or estate assignment, discuss the required document with the professional requesting it. For a sale, compare purchase amounts for the same ring, with the same stones and accessories included. An insurance replacement figure is not a promised resale amount.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds is at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014.

to describe the ring and discuss timing. Payment choices are cash, bank wire and business check; confirm arrangements for your transaction.
Can I bring a ring without a gemstone report?
Yes. Bring what you have and identify any missing information. The actual ring needs examination; a photograph or a seller's description cannot settle every identification question.
Should I clean or repair the ring first?
Discuss its condition before spending money on repairs or using a cleaning treatment. Keep the stone and setting together, and point out any loose or damaged parts when presenting the ring.

children.text: Explain your deadline when arranging the visit

Gather the watch and its history

Bring the watch, original box, warranty card or papers, available service invoices and any spare bracelet links. Keep the documents together and explain anything that does not appear to match. Missing papers are a point to discuss, rather than a reason to invent the watch's history.
Note whether the watch runs, stops or has a known fault.
Disclose replacement parts and aftermarket diamonds or other modifications.
Bring records of servicing and repairs when available.

Understand what may need closer examination

A watch's reference, materials, condition and components must agree with its description. Two watches bearing the same model name can differ in configuration and history. A buyer may need more information about a replaced dial, damaged movement or altered bracelet before making an offer.

Payment choices at Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds are cash, bank wire and business check. Tell us your preference in advance, particularly for a high-value watch or collection. Confirm the final amount, payment timing and receipt arrangements before handing over ownership.

The store is at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Call 310-663-1340 to arrange your evaluation. Bring a list if you are presenting several watches so each watch, its paperwork and its offer can be kept together.
Can every luxury-watch sale be completed the same day?
Completion depends on the actual watch, the required evaluation and agreed payment arrangements. Confirm those details with the store for your visit instead of relying on a general time estimate.
What if my watch needs repair?
Describe the fault when you contact us and bring available repair records. Ask whether the watch can be evaluated in its current condition before paying for work that may not be recovered in a sale.

children.text: Compare the offer for the items you actually own

Choosing a gold buyer in Downtown Los Angeles starts with a clear evaluation. Ask what was tested, what was weighed, and how those findings affect the final amount. A large advertised price means little if it applies to a different purity, excludes some of your items, or changes after deductions.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys gold jewelry, scrap gold, Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, gold coins, and silver coins at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Bring one piece or discuss a substantial collection. Our
gold-buying service
explains the items we evaluate.
Ask for the weight, purity, and offer basis

A useful comparison identifies the same pieces in each offer. For a mixed lot, ask whether 10K, 14K, 18K, and other purities are recorded separately. Confirm the weight unit and how diamonds, springs, or other components affect the metal weight used.
Karat describes the proportion of gold in an alloy: 14K means 14 parts out of 24. Gold plating and gold-filled construction describe different materials. The
FTC guide to jewelry markings
explains these distinctions. A visible stamp is a starting point for an examination, rather than a substitute for testing the item.
Items included:
Are both quotes for the complete lot or only selected pieces?
Measured weight:
Are the units and treatment of non-gold components clear?
Tested purity:
Is the buyer explaining different karats and any uncertain components?
Net payment:
What is the final amount after any stated charges, and how will it be paid?
For the calculation behind an estimate, see
how gold is valued
. There is no universal payout percentage that establishes a fair offer for every item.
Give jewelry and coins the appropriate evaluation

A broken unbranded chain, a diamond-set Cuban bracelet, and a collectible gold coin need different discussions. Ask whether an item is being considered for its metal, its stones, or resale as a complete piece. Avoid dismantling jewelry or removing diamonds before that discussion.

children.text: Bring existing diamond reports, maker documentation, and coin inventory notes with the matching items. Those records help identify what you have; they do not guarantee a premium. Keep potentially collectible coins in their holders and mention any known history.
The
World Gold Council's purity and fineness guide
is useful when interpreting karat and fineness markings. Our
coin-buyer guide
covers questions specific to coin collections.
Choose a selling process you can evaluate

An in-person visit lets you ask questions while the buyer examines your property. A mail-in service involves shipping, receipt, an evaluation period, and written acceptance or return terms. Before using either option, establish what happens if you decline an offer and when your property or payment will be returned.

An outright sale also differs from a pawn loan: a loan has repayment terms and the item serves as security. Compare the transaction you actually want. The business category alone does not establish which buyer will make the better offer.

For heavy Cuban chains, substantial scrap lots, or quantities of gold and silver coins, call
before your visit. Describe the types of items and approximate quantity so the visit and evaluation can be coordinated. Keep separate collections labeled and make your own item list.

Payment is available by cash, bank wire, or business check. Discuss the method and timing before accepting an offer, especially for a high-value transaction. A bank wire or check may have bank processing or availability times; clarify those details rather than assuming every payment method works identically.
Questions before your first visit
Is a purchase offer the same as an insurance appraisal?
No. A purchase offer states what a buyer is willing to pay. An insurance appraisal serves a different purpose and may use a different value basis. Say what you need before arranging an evaluation.
What if I only want to sell some of the items?
Identify those pieces before accepting. Ask for a revised amount for the selected items, because a quote for a full collection may not apply unchanged to a smaller group.
What should I confirm before traveling to Hill Street?
Confirm your visit time, the items you want evaluated, any requested identification or documents, and your preferred payment method. Our
contact page
provides the Downtown Los Angeles location and appointment options.

children.text: Identify what each offer actually covers

Make a list of the coins being offered for sale. Record the country, denomination, year and any visible mint mark when you can read them confidently. Include the number of coins and whether each is in a grading holder or original packaging. Mark uncertain identifications for review.

A quote for an entire collection cannot be compared directly with a quote for its most desirable pieces. If you may sell only part of the collection, ask for that group to be identified separately. Our
coin preparation checklist
helps you organize the visit.
Use fine-gold content, not total weight alone
A gold coin can contain an alloy while still holding a stated amount of fine gold. The
U.S. Mint's bullion specifications

explain that the one-ounce American Gold Eagle contains one troy ounce of gold plus alloy metals. The American Buffalo is a different coin, made from .9999 fine gold. Do not multiply an Eagle's stated one-ounce gold content by its purity again.

For an unfamiliar coin, establish the issue and its specifications before calculating. Face value, gross scale weight and fine-metal content describe different things. A replica or plated piece must not be assigned the composition of the genuine coin it resembles.
Ask whether collectible characteristics were considered

A metal-content estimate is a starting point for discussing bullion. A coin's condition, particular issue, grading information and potential collector interest may need additional review. Age alone does not prove rarity or a premium.

body.alt: Gold bullion bars and gold coins
body.caption: Gold bullion bars and gold coins.

children.text: Keep holders, labels and records together. Do not clean a coin or break it out of a holder merely to make the collection easier to weigh. Ask the buyer to explain whether the offer treats a piece as bullion or recognizes additional collectible characteristics.
Compare a dated reference with a real offer
The
World Gold Council publishes gold-price reference data
. Note the currency, unit and time of a reference before using it. A market price for gold is not a guaranteed bid for an individual coin or unidentified collection.
Are both offers for the same coins and quantity?
Was fine-gold content established for each relevant issue?
Is any premium included, and what supports it?
Are charges, conditions and the final payment amount clear?

children.text: Define the purpose before booking

Begin with what you need to decide or document. You may want a proposal to buy a diamond, a valuation for an insurer, or a report requested by another professional. Those requests should not all be described simply as “an appraisal.”

If a third party needs the report, ask that recipient for its requirements before commissioning work. Tell the appraiser the intended use and valuation date. Do not assume that a report made for an earlier purpose will be accepted for a different one.
Ask about the person's relevant qualifications
GIA's appraisal guidance
distinguishes gemological knowledge from appraisal training. Ask the individual to explain both their stone-identification background and the valuation qualifications relevant to the assignment.

Request the exact credential and issuing organization so you can verify the claim. Ask about experience with your type of jewelry, such as an antique mounting, a colored diamond or a large collection. An impressive general title is less useful than an answer about the actual work.
GIA states that its reports and educational awards are not GIA certification of a business or gemstone
. A reference to GIA education should identify the credential accurately rather than suggest GIA endorsement of the appraisal.
Agree on the report and examination

Ask for a description or sample of the report format. Confirm which items will be examined, which documents you should bring and how each item will be identified in the resulting report. For a collection, agree whether values will be itemized.

Confirm fees, timing and buying interests

Request the fee basis, expected delivery and any additional charges before work begins. Describe the number and complexity of the pieces so the appraiser can answer for your actual collection. A general article cannot supply a reliable quote for every assignment.

Ask whether the appraiser also proposes to buy the item or has another interest in the transaction. If you need an independent valuation, explain that requirement explicitly. Keep any separate purchase proposal clearly labeled.

children.text: Selling Cuban bracelets, bangles, and broken gold

A heavy bracelet can contain substantial gold, but its size alone does not establish its value. A useful evaluation considers its tested purity, metal weight, construction, condition, and any diamonds. Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys Cuban bracelets with or without diamonds, plain gold bangles, and scrap gold in Downtown Los Angeles.
Bring the complete bracelet, including detached links or a broken clasp. If you have matching chains or other unwanted pieces, they can be discussed together through our
gold and jewelry buying service
Why Cuban-link construction matters

Two bracelets of similar width can have different weights. Hollow links contain less metal than comparable solid links, while clasps and repairs may introduce components that need separate examination. Ask which parts are included in the gold calculation rather than treating the entire scale reading as pure gold.

For example, 14K describes an alloy containing 14 parts gold out of 24; it does not mean every gram of the bracelet is pure gold. A gold-plated or gold-filled item has a different construction from karat-gold jewelry. The
FTC's explanation of gold markings and plating
helps distinguish these terms.
Keep any purchase receipt that identifies the material, and point out known repairs. If you are also selling a matching chain, our
14K and Cuban-chain guide
explains the same weight and construction questions in more detail.
Evaluate diamond-set bracelets as complete pieces

A diamond-set Cuban bracelet needs more than a gold-weight calculation. Ask how the stones are identified and whether their contribution is included in the offer. Total diamond weight across many small stones does not describe the size or quality of any individual diamond.

body.alt: Textured gold bracelet on a display cushion
body.caption: Textured gold bracelet on a display cushion.

children.text: Diamond quality involves carat weight, color, clarity, and cut, as explained in
GIA's diamond quality guide

Do not remove stones yourself. Request an evaluation of the complete bracelet first, then clarify the terms of any proposed disassembly. Our
diamond-buying service
provides a starting point for discussing significant stones.
Broken, vintage, and signed bracelets need different attention

A broken clasp does not remove the gold already present in a bracelet. For a piece evaluated primarily for metal, tested purity and recoverable gold weight remain central. Damage can nevertheless affect the value of jewelry that might otherwise be resold intact.

Keep maker marks, original boxes, and useful history with a signed or antique bracelet. Do not assume an inherited piece should be sold only as scrap. Ask whether the design, condition, or maker gives the complete item a resale opportunity before authorizing repairs, polishing, or dismantling.
For a mixture of damaged jewelry, single earrings, and detached links, use our
scrap-gold preparation guide
. Keep separate pieces organized so you can follow the evaluation.
Compare the final amount for the same bracelets

Ask each buyer to identify the pieces, tested karats, weight units, treatment of stones, and net payment. A per-gram quote is only comparable when the material and calculation basis match. An attractive preliminary estimate is not the same as an offer following examination.

There is no single percentage of spot price that proves an offer is fair for every bracelet. A complete jewelry offer can reflect a different resale opportunity from a metal-only purchase. Request an explanation and compare the amount you would receive for the same items.
Bring one bracelet or a substantial collection

Visit Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. We buy heavy Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, scrap gold, gold coins, and silver coins. Large quantities and high-value transactions are welcome.
For a substantial lot,
arrange your visit
and discuss payment beforehand. Payment is available by cash, bank wire, or business check. Confirm the final amount and payment timing before accepting the purchase.
Should I repair a broken bracelet before selling?

Have it evaluated first. A repair may not add enough to the purchase offer to justify its cost, and a vintage or signed piece may need specialist attention. Bring detached components with the bracelet.
Can I sell a bracelet if I do not know its karat?
Yes, you can bring it for evaluation and explain what is unknown. The buyer needs to establish its material before making a meaningful offer; a photograph or color alone cannot confirm gold content.

children.text: Our diamond buying policy

We welcome natural polished diamonds, loose or set in rings, necklaces, bracelets and other jewelry. Any size and any shape can be considered, including substantial individual diamonds and collections. We do not buy laboratory-grown diamonds, uncut crystals or rough diamond material.

If your report identifies a laboratory-grown diamond, it is outside our diamond-buying service. A laboratory name, a high quality assessment or the original purchase amount does not change that policy. See our
large natural diamond buying guide
for the items we buy.
Read the identification before the quality description

Look for the issuing laboratory, report number, date and the wording identifying the stone. Keep the original document with the correct item. Do not assume that a loose report found with inherited jewelry belongs to every diamond in the collection.
GIA explains that natural and laboratory-grown diamonds have essentially similar chemical and optical properties
. Reliable separation can require specialist equipment or laboratory examination. A photograph, sparkle or a basic diamond tester is not enough to establish natural origin.
Understand the GIA assessment date
GIA launched its revised D-to-Z laboratory-grown diamond assessment on
October 1, 2025
. The
official announcement
describes Premium and Standard assessments, with no assessment for stones below the minimum Standard criteria.

body.alt: Close view of a stone being inspected through a loupe
body.caption: Diamond examination tools illustrate the identification process; appearance alone does not establish origin.

children.text: Premium requires D color, VVS clarity or higher, Excellent polish and symmetry, and Excellent cut for round brilliants. Standard uses its own minimum criteria. Read those published criteria rather than assuming that the word Premium covers any color or clarity.

Older documents can use different terminology. Record the date and exact report type instead of converting an older grade into a new description yourself. A terminology change does not turn a laboratory-grown diamond into a natural one.
Check the report and the actual item
For GIA paperwork, use
Report Check

to compare the available record with your document. Then ask how the report number, measurements and identifying information are matched to the actual stone. An online record confirms report information; it does not inspect the item in your possession.

If documentation is missing or unclear, say so. Keep uncertain details marked as unknown. Before paying for new laboratory work, ask what identification is needed and what the service would establish.
A quality assessment is not a purchase offer
A grading or assessment document describes the examined stone. It does not name a buyer or guarantee a resale amount.
GIA distinguishes its reports from monetary appraisals
. An insurance replacement figure and the price originally paid also answer different questions.

If you own a laboratory-grown diamond, review the original retailer's written return or buyback terms and ask any prospective buyer whether it accepts that material before arranging a visit. Do not assume that a policy exists or that another business will buy the stone.
Arrange a natural-diamond evaluation in Downtown LA
For natural polished diamonds, call
or
contact Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds
at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Bring the complete item and existing records. Cash, bank wire and business check are available for agreed purchases.
Do you buy a laboratory-grown diamond with a GIA report?
No. We buy natural polished diamonds only. Having a GIA or other laboratory report does not change the material we accept.
Can I tell natural origin from a diamond photograph?
No. Tell us what the documentation says, and explain any uncertainty. Do not describe the stone as natural solely because of its appearance.

children.text: Read purity and construction as separate information
14K gold contains 14 parts gold in 24 parts of alloy. Fineness expresses gold content per thousand; 585 is a commonly used marking for 14K jewelry. The
World Gold Council's purity guide
explains these conventions.
The
FTC describes solid gold

as a gold item that is not hollow. Gold-filled and plated items have a gold layer over another material. Ask for an explicit description when a seller uses “solid gold” loosely to mean something different.
Inspect the ring without damaging it

Look at the inner band, visible seams, underside of the setting and signs of resizing. Note the markings and any worn areas, but do not scratch the ring on ceramic or apply chemicals to prove a claim. A missing stamp can leave uncertainty; it does not establish that the ring is plated.

A heavy ring may contain substantial metal, but weight alone does not identify that metal. Likewise, a nonmagnetic response does not prove gold. Have the actual ring evaluated and ask how the materials and different components were assessed.
Check whether the price is for metal or a complete ring

For a plain band, gold content and net metal weight are central to a metal estimate. For a signed ring or a ring with diamonds, the setting, maker information and stones may need separate consideration. Keep the item intact until that discussion.

children.text: Understand what 22K means
Karat measures the gold proportion in an alloy. Dividing 22 by 24 gives about 91.67%, compared with 75% for 18K. The
World Gold Council's karat and fineness guide
provides the broader purity context. A 916 marking commonly describes approximately 91.6% fineness, but the marking still needs to be assessed against the piece.

Color is not a purity test. Nor does a high karat guarantee a particular level of resistance to wear: construction, thickness, alloy and use all matter. Do not squeeze a hollow bangle or bend a chain to test whether it is soft.
Keep the full piece separate from its gold content
A scale weighs stones, attachments and other components together with the gold alloy. Ask what weight is used in a metal estimate. The
FTC's jewelry descriptions
also distinguish karat-gold pieces from gold-filled and plated materials.

For a material-content example only, 12 grams of verified 22K alloy contains about 11 grams of gold: 12 × 22 ÷ 24. This assumes the full 12 grams is that alloy. It is not a market price or purchase offer, and it excludes any separate stones or components.
Organize sets and inherited pieces carefully

Keep matching necklaces, earrings and bangles together, with receipts or maker records where available. Note damage and previous repairs. Ask whether the complete set or a signed piece needs consideration beyond metal content before separating it into scrap.

children.text: Build a list before doing the calculation

Use one line per item or clearly identified group. Start with a description you can match back to the jewelry: “broken yellow chain with detached clasp” is more useful than “miscellaneous gold.” Keep a photograph or count for your own records.

The

Do not include gemstone weight as though it were gold alloy. Repairs, springs and other components can also change the applicable weight. Ask the buyer which measurement and purity were used before comparing calculations.
Work through a clearly hypothetical example

Suppose a plain piece contains 10 grams of verified 18K alloy, with no other components in that measurement. Its fine-gold content is 10 × 18 ÷ 24 = 7.5 grams. If a hypothetical pure-gold reference were $100 per gram, the reference metal value would be $750.

children.text: Ask the buyer to identify the complete watch

Start with the model and reference if you know them, but do not guess a reference from a similar online photograph. Describe the dial, bezel, bracelet and material shown in your records. Bring the watch so its actual configuration can be examined.
The
official Rolex Day-Date collection
provides a manufacturer reference for that family. It is not an appraisal of an older watch or proof that a particular item matches the advertised configuration.
Keep metal content and watch value separate

A watch contains a movement, crystal and other components. Its entire measured weight is not the weight of pure gold. The case, bracelet and replacement components also need their own material descriptions.
The
FTC explains gold terminology
, including the difference between an alloy and a surface coating. If metal content is discussed, ask which components and verified fineness the calculation concerns. Our
gold valuation guide
explains the calculation without treating a luxury watch as one solid lump of gold.
Look for a clear account of condition

Ask about bracelet wear, missing links, case shape, dial condition, operation and known repairs. Disclose any aftermarket gem setting, replaced bezel or service work. A manufacturer service replacement and an aftermarket alteration should not be silently grouped together.

children.text: Request an evaluation before paying for cosmetic work. A repair expense does not guarantee an equal increase in a buying offer. Keep service estimates separate from the actual price proposed for the watch as presented.
Bring documents without assigning a fixed premium

Original purchase records, warranty papers, service invoices and spare links help describe what is included. Check that they belong to the watch. Missing paperwork does not prevent you from requesting an evaluation.
No universal percentage applies to a box, a warranty card or a complete package. Ask how the actual accessories were considered rather than adding a predetermined amount to an online asking price.
Compare like-for-like proposals

Record the buyer, evaluation date, included items, final amount and any conditions. Ask whether further inspection could change the figure and whether a fee applies if you decline. Verify individual qualifications or affiliations directly instead of relying on an unsourced ranking.

title: 14K Gold Rings: Compare Design, Materials & Resale

body.alt: Architectural yellow-gold ring with a large square step-cut diamond
body.caption: Architectural yellow-gold ring with a large square step-cut diamond. Illustrative editorial image; not actual inventory or evidence of gemstone identity, purity, coin denomination or geographic origin.

children.text: Compare the same kind of ring

A plain band, a hollow fashion ring and a diamond-set ring can all be described as 14K. Their weights, construction and price components differ. Ask for a written material description and compare rings with similar size, width and stone specifications before drawing conclusions from price.
For the distinction between karat and construction, see our
14K solid-gold ring guide
. The
FTC's jewelry guidance
explains material descriptions and recommends reviewing written seller policies.
Choose color with the finish and alloy in mind
Yellow, white and rose gold can each be made as 14K alloys. The
World Gold Council describes how alloying affects gold color
and notes the common rhodium finish on white gold. The same karat does not establish the same alloy formula or maintenance needs.

Ask about the actual finish and the work involved in maintaining it. If particular metals cause you skin problems, request the alloy information rather than relying on the color or karat as a guarantee.
Inspect fit, setting and stone information

Check whether the band is comfortable, whether neighboring rings rub, and what resizing is possible for the design. Ask how a resize could affect the setting or surface pattern. Thin sections and worn prongs deserve attention even when the gold purity is known.

body.alt: Two gold bands on a dark surface
body.caption: Two gold bands on a dark surface.

children.text: For a ring with a diamond, ask whether it is natural or laboratory-grown, which report describes it, and whether the stated weight is for one stone or all stones combined. The setting's 14K label does not answer those questions.
Keep buying terms separate from resale expectations

Read the return, sizing and warranty terms for the exact purchase, including any customized work. Keep the receipt and matching stone reports. A buyback or trade-in offer, if available from a seller, should be understood on its written terms rather than assumed.
When you later sell, a buyer evaluates the ring you own under then-current conditions. A purchase offer need not match its retail cost or insurance replacement figure. Our
metal-and-diamond value guide
explains why both components matter.

title: Diamond Grading Chart: Read Color, Clarity, Cut & Carat

body.alt: Loose polished diamonds with a jeweler loupe and tweezers
body.caption: Loose polished diamonds with a jeweler loupe and tweezers. Representative editorial image; not a record of this business’s inventory, staff, prices or verified material grades.

children.text: Identify what the chart is showing

Start with the heading and legend. A color scale, a diagram of clarity characteristics and a seller’s price grid answer different questions. Record the laboratory, report type and date before comparing their terminology.

cells: The grade on the stated color scale
Whether the report concerns a D-to-Z or fancy-color diamond
The actual stone, plotted features and report comments
A cut-quality grade where the report provides one
Shape, cutting style, polish and symmetry
Millimeter measurements and any total-weight wording

children.text: A useful comparison keeps the complete description together. Writing only “one carat, good quality” leaves out the details needed to understand the stone.
Read the D-to-Z color scale
The
GIA color guide
describes grading under controlled conditions against reference stones. The familiar groupings below are a reading aid; a screen image cannot reproduce those grading conditions.

body.alt: Existing diamond color scale diagram
body.caption: Existing diamond color scale diagram.

children.text: Use the actual grade on the matching report. Do not assume that everyone sees the same difference between two grades or that a photograph establishes a grade. Fancy-color descriptions need their own context; they should not be forced into this chart.
Decode clarity abbreviations
GIA’s clarity scale
has 11 grades and uses examination under 10× magnification. Characteristics are considered by their size, number, position, nature and relief, rather than by counting marks alone.

“Eye-clean” is not one of these grades. If a seller uses that phrase, ask what viewing conditions it describes and inspect the actual stone. A clarity abbreviation alone is not a promise that a feature will be invisible to you.
Match the chart to the report type
GIA’s sample natural-diamond reports

show how quality information is recorded. The overall GIA cut grade applies to standard round brilliant diamonds in the D-to-Z color range; a missing overall cut grade on another shape does not mean that the stone received a poor grade.
Check laboratory-grown documents separately. GIA’s current
Laboratory-Grown Diamond Quality Assessment
uses Premium or Standard descriptions. Older documents and other report types may use different wording. Read the actual document instead of assuming that one grading chart fits every report.
Keep quality descriptions separate from money
A grade chart is not a quote.
GIA explains that it does not provide monetary appraisals or participate in diamond pricing
. A retail listing, an insurance replacement value and a buyer’s purchase offer therefore should not be treated as interchangeable amounts.
For a sale, ask what the offer includes: the center diamond, accent stones, setting and any associated jewelry. Bring the existing report and explain repairs or changes you know about. The
carat-weight guide
helps separate a single stone’s weight from the combined weight in a ring.
Bring the chart questions to your evaluation
Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys natural polished diamonds of any size and shape at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. We do not buy laboratory-grown, uncut or rough diamonds. Review our
diamond-buying service
and
contact us
with the item and paperwork you have. Ask for an explanation of the final offer for your actual piece.
Can I grade my diamond from an online chart?
You can learn the terminology and prepare questions. The chart does not replace examination of the stone under the required grading conditions.
Does a report number guarantee the price?
No. A report supplies information about the examined stone. Confirm that it matches your item and ask the buyer to state a separate purchase amount.

title: How to Value Estate Jewelry: Inventory, Materials & Records

body.alt: A substantial three-stone diamond ring beside a closed jeweler's loupe on a warm gray evaluation pad
body.caption: A substantial three-stone diamond ring beside a closed jeweler's loupe on a warm gray evaluation pad. Illustrative estate-style jewelry; not authenticated age, actual inventory or grading evidence.

children.text: Create a simple inventory before assigning values

Give each piece a short identifier and photograph it from several angles. Keep matching earrings, chains and pendants associated with one another, and note any detached parts. Separate observations from assumptions: “blue stone” is more useful than an unsupported claim that it is sapphire.

cells: Ring A, necklace B or another clear label
Letters, numbers and symbols exactly as seen
Missing pieces, damage and known repairs
Receipts, reports, appraisals and maker information
Documented facts, with family recollections labeled separately

children.text: Keep materials and complete-piece features separate

A collection may contain precious metals, plated items, costume jewelry and pieces whose materials are unknown. Do not assume that everything is gold because it came from the same jewelry box. Let examination establish which materials are present.

body.alt: Assorted colored gemstone rings in a display tray
body.caption: Assorted colored gemstone rings in a display tray.

children.text: For gold jewelry, the relevant metal weight and purity must be distinguished from stones and other components. A complete piece also warrants consideration of its design and condition.
GIA’s estate jewelry guide
highlights examination for damage, missing stones and evidence of repairs.
Ask what supports stone and maker identification

Bring existing laboratory reports and ask which stones they describe. Natural origin and treatment status are separate details; an identification should not assume that every natural gemstone is untreated. Record what the examiner established and any limits on the assessment.
If a report describes a diamond, our
diamond grading chart guide
explains its color, clarity and cut terminology so you can prepare more specific evaluation questions.

A maker’s mark or period-style design can guide research, but it is not a substitute for authentication. Ask what supports the attribution and date. Avoid dismantling a possible antique or signed piece before its complete design has been considered; see the
antique gold evaluation guide
Define the purpose of a requested value
The
Appraisal Foundation’s jewelry guide
explains that a credible appraisal identifies the items, intended use, value definition and relevant date. Establish those requirements before commissioning a report.

A buyer’s current purchase amount answers a different practical question: what is offered for the stated items under the stated terms? Do not convert an old appraisal into that amount using a fixed percentage. Our
inherited jewelry documentation guide
helps you choose the right next step.
Preserve the collection for evaluation
Store pieces separately and avoid experimenting with cleaning on unfamiliar materials.
GIA’s care guidance
notes that gemstones and treatments can require different handling. Ask before paying for restoration intended only to improve a sale price.
For a purchase evaluation,
contact Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds
at 310-663-1340 or visit 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Our
estate jewelry service
can discuss the collection you have and the information needed for an offer.
Can I value an entire jewelry box by its total weight?
No. Different materials and individual pieces need identification. A combined scale weight does not establish the relevant precious-metal content or complete-piece value.
Should I discard items that look like costume jewelry?
Keep uncertain items identifiable until you know what they are. Appearance alone is not a reliable way to sort a collection by material or potential significance.

title: Jewelry Buyer Reviews in Los Angeles: How to Read Them

body.alt: A pair of substantial ruby and large pear-shaped diamond drop earrings on ivory silk
body.caption: A pair of substantial ruby and large pear-shaped diamond drop earrings on ivory silk. Illustrative jewelry image; not actual inventory or a representation of verified origin, purity or grading.

children.text: Match the review to the right business and service

Check the business name, location and type of transaction. A review of a jewelry repair or retail purchase may say little about selling a diamond or a mixed estate collection. Similar business names can also make it easy to read feedback about another location.

Record the date of the review and the service described. A useful shortlist should connect the feedback to what you need now: gold buying, a natural diamond evaluation, a luxury watch purchase or an estate jewelry offer.
Use ratings as a starting point for reading
The
FTC’s online review guidance
recommends checking multiple sources and considering recency and reviewer history. It also cautions that readers cannot reliably identify every fake review by appearance alone.

body.alt: Gold-tone necklaces and earrings on display blocks
body.caption: Gold-tone necklaces and earrings on display blocks.

children.text: There is no magic threshold such as a particular star score or number of reviews that proves a buyer is trustworthy. A new business may have few reviews, while a long history of feedback may involve services unrelated to yours. Read the substance before drawing a conclusion.
Turn specific experiences into practical questions

cells: How will my particular items be examined?
Which assumptions could change after inspection?
What timing applies to my preferred payment method?
Will my offer identify included items or selected pieces?
Is that service separate, and what are its terms?

children.text: A reviewer’s outcome is not a promise about your transaction. A larger collection, an unfamiliar stone or a different payment method can require different steps. Ask about the process for your own items instead of assuming an identical timetable or price.
Read complaints and responses in context

Note the specific issue and whether the business response addresses it. Separate a disagreement about the amount offered from an allegation about custody, undisclosed charges or an unfulfilled agreement. Those concerns require different questions.

A repeated concern is a reason to investigate, not enough on its own to declare the business dishonest. Likewise, an enthusiastic comment about a high payout does not reveal the item’s full description. Use our
buyer questions guide
to verify the details directly.
Compare offers after doing the review research
Bring the same items and records to each evaluation. Ask for the final amount, included components, any deductions and the offer’s conditions. Keep that comparison separate from the online rating.
The
Los Angeles jewelry selling options guide
can help you choose the type of buyer or selling arrangement to investigate. Check whether a proposed amount is a purchase offer, a trade-in allowance or an estimate for a future sale.

Contact us
at 310-663-1340 to discuss your jewelry and the next step. Review our
gold buying
and
estate jewelry services
for the items you plan to bring.
Does a five-star average guarantee the highest offer?
No. Reviews do not establish an amount for your actual jewelry. Compare the final item-specific offer and its terms.
Should one negative review decide where I sell?
Read what happened, check its relevance and look for context across sources. Use the concern to ask specific questions before agreeing to a transaction.

title: 24K Gold Chains: Fineness, Construction & Selling Guide

body.caption: Thick yellow-gold rope necklace with its clasp on pale limestone. Illustrative jewelry image; appearance does not establish purity or actual inventory.

children.text: Read the fineness description carefully
24K describes essentially pure gold. In practical fineness descriptions, you may see figures such as 999 or 999.9 rather than a promise of absolute purity. The
World Gold Council explains karat and fineness
, including this distinction.

Photograph readable marks on your chain or record them with its paperwork. Ask how the actual chain and its components will be evaluated. Neither yellow color nor a stamp alone proves the composition of the complete necklace.
Inspect the links and clasp as a connected piece

Look for stretched links, flattening, previous repairs and an unreliable clasp. Different link styles use different construction, so identical appearance is not a universal quality test. A wide chain can be hollow or contain less metal than its size suggests.
The
FTC notes that pure gold is soft
. Handle the necklace carefully and avoid bending links to test it. Ask about the condition and construction before paying for polishing or a repair solely to prepare a sale.
Separate the chain from a pendant in your inventory

A pendant may have a different purity, maker or stone from the chain. Keep the set together but ask whether the components need separate evaluation. The same applies to a replacement clasp or a section repaired with different material.

body.alt: Gold chain arranged on pale stone blocks
body.caption: Gold chain arranged on pale stone blocks.

children.text: For a necklace with diamonds, note that the total scale weight includes the stones. Our
chain construction guide
explains why weight and appearance need to be considered together, even though the nominal purity differs.
Compare the actual offer, not a promised return

The retail price of a chain can include design, labor and brand premiums. Those costs are not automatically recovered in a sale. Ask how the buyer considered net metal weight and whether the intact necklace has a separate resale opportunity.

body.caption: Wide white-metal ring with a large rectangular step-cut diamond. Illustrative editorial image; not actual inventory or evidence of gemstone identity, purity, coin denomination or geographic origin.

children.text: Distinguish the alloy from the surface finish
White gold combines gold with other metals to produce a paler alloy. Many pieces also have a rhodium finish. The
World Gold Council's color guide
explains this combination. A bright white surface does not make the ring platinum, and surface wear alone does not establish that the underlying ring is fake.

Record the 14K or fineness marking and keep any material description from the original seller. Ask about the actual alloy if you need to avoid a particular metal; a color name is not an ingredient list.
Review worn areas and previous work

Look at the underside of the band, prongs and areas that rub against another ring. Note resizing, replacement sections or previous refinishing. These details help explain the current condition and any later repair estimate.
Before paying to replate a ring just to sell it, ask whether that work would affect the purchase offer enough to justify the cost. The
FTC's jewelry guidance
is useful for separating gold-alloy and plated-product descriptions.
Keep diamond quality separate from the 14K label
A 14K marking describes the metal, not the diamond. Bring any matching laboratory report and identify whether it describes the center stone or a collection of stones.
GIA's diamond quality guide
explains the separate roles of cut, color, clarity and carat weight.

body.alt: Yellow-gold-tone and white-metal diamond bands
body.caption: Yellow-gold-tone and white-metal diamond bands.

white-gold diamond-ring guide
for the combined metal-and-stone discussion.
Compare offers for the complete ring

Ask what metal weight was used and how the stones, condition and any maker information influenced the amount. Equal weights of equally pure white and yellow gold contain equal quantities of gold; complete jewelry offers can still differ.

children.text: Describe the emerald and the complete ring

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys only large, high-quality gemstones. Green Colombian emeralds are among our focus areas, alongside Burmese rubies and Ceylon blue sapphires. If your emerald ring has no certificate, you can still contact us for an evaluation.

Share the known stone weight or dimensions, the ring’s metal description and any existing records. If the Colombian origin comes from a family account rather than a laboratory report, explain that distinction. Color alone cannot confirm where a gemstone formed.
Consider quality and condition together
GIA’s emerald quality guide

discusses color, clarity, cut and carat weight, including the role of visible inclusions. A large emerald still needs a quality assessment; size by itself does not satisfy our selective gemstone buying focus.

body.alt: Assorted colored gemstone rings in a display tray
body.caption: Assorted colored gemstone rings in a display tray.

children.text: Ask the evaluator to consider the stone’s appearance, condition and any known treatments. An inclusion seen in a photograph is not a complete identification, and an apparently clear stone should not be labeled laboratory-grown without examination.

cells: Known weight or measurements, with estimates labeled
The report, receipt or other source of the claim
Existing information about clarity enhancement or other work
Gold marks, maker information and known repairs
Chips, loose settings or replaced components to examine

children.text: Use existing reports without making them a prerequisite
GIA describes different colored-stone report services
, including identification and reports that also address origin. Read what your actual report covers. A document does not automatically guarantee a particular purchase amount.

Certificates are welcome but not required here. Bring any records you already have and ask what further examination, if any, would be useful before commissioning additional work. Keep natural origin and treatment information as separate questions.
Protect the emerald while preparing the sale
GIA’s emerald care guide

cautions against ultrasonic and steam cleaning because fractures and clarity-enhancement materials can be affected. A hardness number alone should not be treated as permission for rough handling or aggressive cleaning.

Bring the ring intact and disclose any damage you know about. Ask before polishing, repairing or removing the stone solely to prepare a sale. Preserve the complete design and records, especially if it may be an estate or signed piece.

The finished ring’s scale weight includes the emerald and any other components. Ask how the
gold setting
and the gemstone are considered, and whether the offer includes the complete ring. The

Identify the movement and functions

A stopped watch does not reveal the cause by itself. Do not assume a battery change or routine service will resolve every problem. Avoid opening the case or forcing controls on an unfamiliar watch.
Consider wear and complete construction

Examine the bracelet length and available extra links, clasp closure, visible case wear and any known replacement parts. A substantial bracelet and a watch on a leather strap are different packages even when the case designs look similar.

Read color separately from clarity
The

children.text: Clarity is a different characteristic. Calling a stone “clear” does not supply either its formal clarity grade or its color grade. Likewise, a hazy-looking photograph cannot prove that the diamond is Fancy white; the actual stone and the relevant examination are needed.

cells: Is this informal color wording or a report description?

No. A photograph cannot establish that distinction. Have the stone examined and read the appropriate report information.

body.alt: Wide polished white-metal band with one large east-west emerald-cut diamond

children.text: The white color does not identify the material
A pale ring might be white gold, platinum, silver or a plated base metal. Appearance alone cannot reliably distinguish them. Check available marks and paperwork, then have the actual piece examined.
The
World Gold Council describes white-gold alloys and rhodium finishes
. The added metals vary by alloy. A color or karat description does not disclose every ingredient or establish suitability for someone with a metal sensitivity; ask the maker for the composition.
Karat describes the gold proportion

Nominal 14K is 14 parts gold out of 24, approximately 58.33%; 18K is 75%. The remaining alloy can differ even between two pieces with the same karat. Pure gold is naturally yellow, so a white surface is not evidence of pure 24K gold.
For equal net weights of verified alloy, a higher gold fraction means more gold. It does not mean every light 18K ring contains more gold than every heavy 10K ring. See our
14K per-gram explanation
for a worked calculation that separates alloy weight from fine-gold weight.
Rhodium wear and damage are different questions

A bright surface can change as its finish wears. That observation alone cannot tell you whether prongs are sound, a band is thinning or the underlying metal is what a stamp suggests. Have structural concerns examined separately.

body.alt: White-metal solitaire ring worn on a hand
body.caption: White-metal solitaire ring worn on a hand.

children.text: Before paying for replating solely to sell a ring, discuss whether it would affect an actual purchase offer. A fresh finish does not increase the amount of gold in the alloy, and its cost may not be recovered. Bring the ring in its existing condition and disclose known repairs.
Separate gold content from the jewelry offer

Two verified alloys with the same net weight and gold fraction contain the same quantity of gold, regardless of white or yellow color. Their complete-jewelry offers may differ because of stones, design, maker, condition or saleability.
A pure-gold market quote multiplied by the whole ring's weight skips both the alloy fraction and any stones or other materials. Read the
FTC's jewelry descriptions
when distinguishing an alloy from a gold-plated or filled item.
Bring the stone information and matching documents

Keep a report with the diamond it describes, and bring receipts or maker documentation if available. A report describes the stone; it does not turn a metal estimate into a guaranteed purchase amount. Our
white-gold diamond ring guide
covers the setting and stone together.
For an uncertain white-metal piece, our
platinum and white-gold comparison

children.text: Start with the source and timestamp
An article's publication year does not make a quoted price current. Check the observation date and whether a display represents a live quote, a benchmark observation or a historical series. The
World Gold Council's gold-price data
provides a dated reference with its own methodology and units.

This guide explains how to read those inputs. It does not claim to measure Los Angeles jewelry sales or supply a live buying rate for Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds. A local purchase amount requires examination of your items.
Use the same currency and weight unit

A price per troy ounce cannot be multiplied directly by a jewelry weight measured in grams. Likewise, a dollar quote and a quote in another currency cannot be compared without a matching conversion and timestamp. Record the units next to every number before calculating.

If two buyers describe rates differently, ask them to express the final amount for the same actual collection. A higher number per unit does not establish a higher offer when the unit or included material differs.
Apply purity to the right weight
The
World Gold Council's fineness guide
explains gold proportions. Nominal 14K is 14/24, about 58.33%, while a 585 mark denotes a fineness convention of 58.5%. Use the verified input appropriate to the piece and explain any approximation.

body.alt: Gold jewelry arranged beside a digital scale and testing tools
body.caption: Gold jewelry arranged beside a digital scale and testing tools.

children.text: For a simple quantity example, 20 grams of verified 18K alloy contains 15 grams of gold. The calculation assumes the 20 grams excludes stones and other non-alloy components. Multiplying that fine-gold quantity by a compatible market reference produces a theoretical metal amount, not a buyer's commitment.
Our
14K gold-price guide
shows the same distinction for 14K jewelry. Avoid applying the purity factor twice if a rate has already been expressed per gram of that alloy.
Keep other sources of value visible

A signed bracelet, diamond Cuban chain or collectible coin needs questions beyond the bulk gold calculation. Condition and identifying documents can matter to an intact item's resale potential. Coins also require the correct issue and stated metal content.
Ask whether the proposal covers the complete piece, its materials or separate components. Our
valuation guide

coin collection checklist

Use the same pieces and accessories in each evaluation.
Record the tested purity, applicable weight and units.

body.caption: A collection of worn gold jewelry and scrap pieces. Representative editorial image; not a record of this business’s inventory, staff, prices or verified material grades.

children.text: Inspect the piece before choosing a test

Marks, joins, repairs, plating and mixed components give the evaluator clues about what needs examination. A bracelet body and clasp may not be identical material. An unmarked piece can still warrant testing, while a visible karat mark is not conclusive proof.
Tell the buyer about replaced parts or previous work and bring matching records. Keep an intact piece together until the proposed examination has been explained.
Understand what the method can show
GIA's comparison of gold-testing methods
documents limitations as well as useful applications. The right interpretation depends on the method, sample and item; the name of a machine is not itself a guarantee of an exact result.
Surface composition can also be misleading. In a
GIA case study of gold-plated gold
, plating complicated XRF readings of the underlying alloy. Ask how mixed materials or surface layers are addressed when they are relevant.
Before a procedure that could mark, scratch or alter jewelry, discuss what is proposed. Do not assume every testing method is non-destructive or that one reading resolves every question.
Distinguish the scale reading from net alloy weight

The whole-item reading can include stones, springs, steel components or other materials. With a mounted stone, its weight may be estimated unless a matching report or direct measurement supplies better information. Ask which quantities were measured and which remain estimates.

children.text: Convert the price before applying purity
Check the currency, date and unit of a

NIST's mass conversions

For 10K alloy, multiply a fine-gold rate per gram by 10/24. The

Work through a clearly hypothetical example
Suppose the net weight is ten grams of verified 10K alloy, with stones and non-alloy components excluded. Nominal contained gold is 10 × 10 ÷ 24, or approximately 4.1667 grams.

If fine gold were hypothetically $100 per gram, that contained gold would have a theoretical reference amount of about $416.67. This is an illustration, not today's price or a purchase offer. A whole-item scale reading that includes other materials would need further adjustment before using this calculation.
Ask whether the quote already includes the karat adjustment

A buyer may express a proposed rate per gram of verified 10K alloy. That is different from a fine-gold market rate. Applying the 10/24 factor again to an already adjusted 10K rate would reduce it twice.

title: 14K Gold Price Per Gram: Estimating Jewelry Value

body.alt: Gold bars displayed with United States banknotes
body.caption: Gold bars displayed with United States banknotes. Representative editorial image; not a record of this business’s inventory, staff, prices or verified material grades.

children.text: Calculate the gold content before comparing prices

To estimate the metal value of 14K gold, multiply the pure-gold price per gram by 14 ÷ 24, or approximately 0.5833. Then multiply by the net weight of the 14K alloy. This estimates contained gold value; a purchase offer also depends on the actual item and the buyer's terms.
14K means 14 parts gold in a 24-part alloy. A 585 fineness mark indicates 58.5% gold and is commonly associated with 14K jewelry. The
World Gold Council's explanation of karat and fineness
describes the small distinction between nominal 14K and 585. Use the purity established during the evaluation when comparing a real offer. Our guide to
14K marks, color and construction
explains what these descriptions tell you.

A marking is a starting clue: stamps can wear, repairs can introduce other metals, and separate components may have different purities. Ask how purity will be checked and whether a proposed test could mark the piece.
GIA’s 1992 study of gold-testing methods
provides historical background on touchstone, electronic and X-ray fluorescence (XRF) testing and their limitations.
Convert a troy-ounce reference into grams
If a gold-price reference is quoted in dollars per troy ounce, first divide it by 31.1034768 to obtain dollars per gram of pure gold. A troy ounce is different from an ordinary household ounce. The
NIST mass reference
provides the conversion.
Estimated contained gold value = net alloy weight in grams × tested gold fraction × pure-gold price per gram.
The
World Gold Council's gold-price data

offers market references. Check the currency, unit, date, and whether a displayed value is an average or benchmark. It is not a binding offer for your jewelry, and this article does not display a live buying rate.
Worked example: a 25-gram 14K bracelet

Assume a plain bracelet contains 25 grams of 14K alloy after accounting for any non-gold components. Its estimated pure-gold content is 25 × 14 ÷ 24 = approximately 14.58 grams. Multiply that amount by the current reference price per gram of pure gold to obtain a metal-content estimate.

body.caption: Gold jewelry arranged beside a digital scale and testing tools.

children.text: These are calculated metal quantities, not promised payouts. A bracelet's total weight may also include diamonds, non-gold springs, or other materials. A household scale and a visible stamp can help you prepare questions, but they do not establish a tested net gold weight.
Understand the difference between a reference and an offer

A metal-only purchase offer can reflect testing, processing, refining, resale costs, and the buyer's margin. Jewelry with a desirable maker, significant stones, or collectible features may instead deserve evaluation as a complete piece. Do not add an intact jewelry resale estimate to its full metal value; that could count the same material twice. To distinguish a retail receipt or replacement appraisal from a current offer, read
what to expect for gold jewelry

For heavy Cuban chains and bracelets, ask about construction as well as weight. Hollow links and solid links can look similar while containing different amounts of metal. If diamonds are present, ask how the stones affect both the weight calculation and the offer. See our
14K chain guide
for these item-specific checks.
Compare 14K gold offers on the same basis

Keep the same pieces together when requesting comparisons. Ask each buyer to state the tested purity, weight unit, weight used, whether stones are included, any charges, and the final payment. If one quote uses grams and another uses pennyweights, ask for matching units before comparing rates. Use the
gold-offer comparison worksheet
to record the same details for each buyer.
An estimate given before examination may change if the item differs from the description. Compare final amounts for the actual jewelry, not only an advertised per-gram figure. Our
gold-valuation guide
covers the broader factors behind an offer.

covers what to bring. Call

for the full buying scope.
Are equal weights of 14K white, yellow and rose gold worth the same?
At the same tested gold fraction, they contain the same amount of gold. A complete piece's offer may still differ because of its stones, maker, condition, or resale demand. Read more about
white gold's alloy and finish
Should I remove stones before weighing my jewelry?
No. Have the intact jewelry evaluated first and ask how non-gold weight is accounted for. Removing stones can damage the setting and make an evaluation of the complete piece more difficult.
Can this formula tell me the best day to sell?
No. It explains metal content using a stated price reference; it does not predict markets. Decide using an actual offer, the items you own, and your circumstances.

children.text: Compare equal quantities of the same purity

Color does not set the karat. A white 14K ring and a yellow 18K ring have different nominal gold fractions; two verified 14K alloys share the same nominal fraction but may have different weights. Keep both inputs visible before comparing their gold content.
The

Look at the finish as well as the underlying alloy

Many white-gold pieces have a bright rhodium surface. Wear can change that appearance without changing the stated gold proportion of the underlying alloy. Yellow-gold pieces also need inspection for wear, repairs and structural condition.
There is no universal replating schedule or maintenance cost for every ring. Ask the maker or jeweler about the specific finish and your pattern of wear. Our
white-gold guide
explains the alloy-versus-surface distinction.
Choose appearance by the actual piece

Compare the jewelry in ordinary lighting and alongside pieces you wear. A bright polished surface, a matte finish and a diamond setting can change the overall appearance as much as the broad color name. Personal preference is more useful than a rule assigning one metal to a particular skin tone.

Ask about composition and construction

Likewise, do not infer sturdiness from color. Band thickness, hollow or solid construction, worn sections and the setting all deserve inspection. The
FTC distinguishes construction and metal-quality descriptions
Compare complete-jewelry offers separately from gold content

A diamond, recognized maker, unusual design or condition difference can affect an intact item's resale potential. There is no fixed color premium that can establish the offer for two different pieces, and retail price differences do not automatically carry over to resale.

For an inherited watch, keep family information distinct from documented history and confirm your authority to decide about a sale. The

children.text: A receipt records what was bought then

A retail price can include design, manufacture, distribution and the terms of that original sale. It is not a promise that a buyer will later purchase the piece for the same amount or a standard fraction of it.
Bring the receipt if it helps identify the item, maker or specifications. Use it as supporting information rather than treating the original total as today's minimum purchase amount.
A metal estimate needs verified inputs
Nominal 14K is 14 parts gold out of 24, and 18K is 18 out of 24. The
World Gold Council's fineness guide
explains those proportions. For equal net alloy weights, the higher fraction contains more gold; for different weights, both inputs are needed.
A
dated fine-gold reference price
can inform a theoretical material amount. Apply it to contained gold, not automatically to the gross weight of jewelry with stones or other components. Our
valuation checklist

The complete item can need a different evaluation

A broken chain still contains its remaining gold. A signed estate jewel, diamond Cuban bracelet or collectible watch may also have characteristics relevant to resale as an intact piece. Ask about those before treating the whole collection as scrap.

A fixed percentage cannot define every reasonable offer

Material form, verified information, resale potential, business costs and transaction terms can differ. An article cannot establish a minimum or maximum fair percentage for every buyer and piece. A higher or lower number needs context before it can be assessed.

Ask whether the amount is final, which pieces it covers and whether charges or further checks remain. If one quote excludes a diamond while another includes it, resolve that difference before comparing totals. The

Bring the actual material, including uncertain pieces
A stamp can guide examination but does not establish authenticity by itself. The
FTC explains gold alloy, filled and plated descriptions
. A plated item's entire weight should not be valued as though it were a solid gold alloy.

Keep broken parts with their matching items and avoid unnecessary polishing or dismantling before the evaluation. Original paperwork is useful when available; ask what identification and transaction documents are needed.

title: Where to Sell Gold in Los Angeles: A Seller’s Checklist

body.alt: Thick braided gold chain with a substantial matching bracelet
body.caption: Thick braided gold chain with a substantial matching bracelet. Illustrative editorial image; not actual inventory or evidence of gemstone identity, purity, coin denomination or geographic origin.

children.text: If you’re wondering
where to sell gold in Los Angeles

, the best place is not necessarily the buyer advertising the biggest number. The better choice is a reputable gold buyer who clearly explains how your gold is tested, weighed, and valued before you decide whether to sell.

Los Angeles has many options for selling gold, including pawn shops, jewelry stores, precious-metal dealers, and dedicated gold buyers. Understanding how these businesses calculate an offer can help you compare buyers and make a more informed decision.
At
Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds
, we believe sellers should understand what affects the value of their gold before accepting an offer.
Where Can You Sell Gold in Los Angeles?
Los Angeles sellers generally have several options.
Professional Gold Buyers
A professional gold buyer specializes in evaluating precious metals and may purchase gold jewelry, broken jewelry, coins, bullion, dental gold, and other gold items.
A knowledgeable buyer should be able to explain the testing and valuation process so you understand how the offer was determined.
Pawn Shops
Pawn shops commonly purchase gold and may be convenient when someone wants to sell an item quickly.

However, offers can vary significantly from one shop to another. A pawn shop also operates a broader business involving many types of merchandise, whereas a precious-metals buyer may have more specialized experience evaluating gold.
If you’re considering this option, see our guide on
How Much Do Pawn Shops Pay for Gold? What Los Angeles Sellers Should Know
Jewelry Stores
Some jewelry stores purchase used gold jewelry, although buying gold from the public may not be their primary business.
This can be an option for certain pieces, but sellers should ask whether the item is being valued primarily for its gold content, its resale potential, or both.
Online Gold Buyers
Online buyers allow sellers to mail their gold for evaluation.

This can be convenient, but it means temporarily giving up possession of your jewelry before receiving an offer. Before mailing valuable items, carefully review the company’s shipping procedures, insurance coverage, return policy, reputation, and payment terms.
How Is the Value of Your Gold Calculated?
Several factors determine what your gold may be worth.
Gold Purity
Gold jewelry is commonly marked according to karat purity.
Examples include:
10K gold
14K gold
18K gold
22K gold
24K gold
Pure gold is 24 karat. Lower-karat jewelry contains gold mixed with other metals.
For example, 14K gold contains a smaller percentage of pure gold than 18K gold. Because of that difference, two pieces with the same weight can have different underlying gold values.
The
Federal Trade Commission explains common gold, plated and filled jewelry descriptions
. Use the description as a starting point and have the actual material evaluated.
Weight
After determining purity, the weight of the gold becomes another major factor.

Professional buyers generally weigh gold using a calibrated scale. Stones, non-gold components, and other materials may need to be considered separately when determining the amount of actual gold in an item.
Current Gold Market Price
Gold is traded internationally, and its market price changes over time.
The current gold price provides an important reference point when determining the underlying metal value of an item. The
World Gold Council publishes dated gold-price information
. Check the date, currency and unit before using a quote as a reference.

However, the market price of pure gold should not be confused with the amount a buyer will necessarily offer for jewelry. Buyers must consider purity, refining or resale costs, operating expenses, and other factors.
Does a Gold Buyer Pay the Full Spot Price?
Usually, you should not expect a buyer to simply multiply the item’s total weight by the quoted price of pure gold.

body.alt: Gold jewelry arranged beside a digital scale and testing tools
body.caption: Gold jewelry arranged beside a digital scale and testing tools.

children.text: The advertised spot price generally refers to pure gold in the wholesale market. Most jewelry is not 24K pure gold.
For example, a 14K necklace contains gold as well as other metals. Its theoretical precious-metal value therefore differs from the value of the same weight in pure 24K gold.
A buyer’s actual offer can also reflect testing, processing, refining, resale potential, and the buyer’s operating margin.
This is why comparing offers based only on a percentage advertised in an ad can be misleading.
How Can You Get the Best Price When Selling Gold in Los Angeles?
You don’t need to be a precious-metals expert to make a better-informed decision.
Know What You Have
Before visiting a buyer, look for karat markings such as 10K, 14K, 18K, 22K, or 24K.
Keep in mind that a stamp is useful information but may still need to be professionally verified.
Separate Different Karats
If you have several pieces, consider separating them according to their marked purity before the evaluation.
Different karats should generally not be treated as though they contain the same amount of gold.
Ask to See the Weight
A transparent evaluation should allow you to understand the weight being used to calculate your offer.
Ask what unit of measurement is being used and whether stones or non-gold components affect the calculation.
Ask How Purity Is Tested
Gold can be evaluated using several methods depending on the item and buyer.
Ask the buyer how they determine purity and whether the testing can be explained to you during the evaluation.
Compare More Than One Offer
If you are uncertain about an offer, you can obtain another evaluation before selling.
Gold jewelry is valuable property. You should feel comfortable understanding the offer before making your decision.
What Types of Gold Can You Sell?
Depending on the buyer, you may be able to sell:
Gold necklaces
Gold bracelets
Gold rings
Gold earrings
Broken gold jewelry
Unwanted jewelry
Scrap gold
Gold coins
Gold bullion
Gold watches
Dental gold
Estate jewelry
Don’t assume an item has no value simply because it is broken, outdated, tangled, or missing stones. Its precious-metal content may still have value.
Should You Sell Broken Gold Jewelry?
Broken gold can still have significant value because the underlying gold does not cease to be valuable simply because the jewelry can no longer be worn.
Broken chains, single earrings, damaged bracelets, bent rings, and other unwanted pieces can potentially be evaluated according to their precious-metal content.
Before throwing damaged jewelry away, consider having it evaluated.
What About Designer or Estate Jewelry?
Not every piece should automatically be treated as scrap gold.
Certain designer jewelry, antique pieces, estate jewelry, watches, gemstones, and collectible items may have value beyond their precious-metal content.
A knowledgeable buyer should recognize when an item deserves additional evaluation rather than automatically treating everything as scrap.
This is particularly important when selling inherited jewelry or an estate collection when you may not know the history or significance of individual pieces.
What Should You Bring When Selling Gold?
Bring the gold items you want evaluated along with any documentation you have that may be relevant.
For certain jewelry, watches, coins, or collectible pieces, useful documentation can include original receipts, boxes, certificates, grading reports, or previous appraisals.
Documentation isn’t always necessary to evaluate ordinary gold jewelry, but it can be useful for pieces whose value may extend beyond their metal content.
Also bring valid identification if required for the transaction.
Questions to Ask a Gold Buyer Before Selling
Before accepting an offer, consider asking:
How did you determine the purity?
The buyer should be able to explain how the gold was tested.
What weight are you using?
Make sure you understand the weight used in the calculation.
What gold price are you referencing?
Because the market changes, ask what reference price is being used at the time of your evaluation.
Are gemstones or collectible value included?
If your jewelry contains diamonds, gemstones, or has potential designer or collectible value, ask whether those factors were considered separately.
Is the evaluation free?
Ask whether there is any obligation or fee before agreeing to an evaluation.
Red Flags When Choosing a Gold Buyer
Be cautious when a buyer:
Refuses to explain how an offer was calculated
Will not let you see or understand the weighing process
Pressures you to sell immediately
Makes claims that sound unrealistic
Provides unclear information about the business
Cannot explain how purity was determined
A legitimate transaction should give you enough information to make your own decision.
Is It Better to Sell Gold Locally in Los Angeles?
For many sellers, working with a local buyer has an important advantage: you can have the item evaluated while you are present.
You can ask questions, understand the testing process, receive an offer, and decide whether you want to proceed without mailing your valuables away.
Los Angeles also has a large jewelry and precious-metals market, giving sellers multiple options when comparing evaluations.
Where Can I Sell Gold Near Me in Los Angeles?

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds is at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. We buy scrap gold, Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, gold jewelry, gold coins and silver coins. Single pieces and large quantities are welcome.
